t.6.1: The Blessed Lord said: He who performs the work that ought to be done, without depending on the fruit of action, is both a renunciant and a yogī; not he who is without the sacred fire, nor he who is without action.
t.6.2: What they call renunciation, know that to be yoga, O Pāṇḍava; for no one becomes a yogī who has not renounced his intentions.
t.6.3: For the sage who wishes to ascend to yoga, action is said to be the means; for that same one, once he has ascended to yoga, tranquility is said to be the means.
t.6.4: For when one is attached neither to the objects of the senses nor to actions, and has renounced all intentions, then he is said to have ascended to yoga.
t.6.5: One should lift oneself up by oneself; one should not let oneself sink down. For the self alone is the friend of the self, and the self alone is the enemy of the self.
t.6.6: For him by whom the self has been conquered by the self, the self is a friend of the self; but for one who has not conquered himself, the self would remain in enmity, just like an enemy.
t.6.7: For one who has conquered himself and is perfectly tranquil, the supreme Self remains steadfastly composed in cold and heat, in pleasure and pain, and likewise in honor and dishonor.
t.6.8: The yogī whose self is content with knowledge and realized wisdom, who stands unshaken like an anvil, who has conquered his senses, and to whom a clod of earth, a stone, and gold are the same, is said to be truly established in yoga.
t.6.9: He who regards with an equal mind well-wishers, friends, enemies, the indifferent, the neutral, the hateful and kinsmen, and even the righteous and the sinful, excels.
t.6.10: The yogī should constantly discipline himself, remaining in seclusion, alone, with mind and self controlled, free from desire and without possessions.
t.6.12: There, having made the mind one-pointed, with the activities of thought and senses restrained, seated upon that seat, let him practise yoga for the purification of the self.
t.6.11: Having set up for himself a firm seat in a clean place, neither too high nor too low, covered with cloth, deerskin and kuśa grass.
t.6.13: Holding the body, head and neck erect and motionless, remaining steady, gazing at the tip of his own nose and not looking around in any direction.
t.6.15: Thus constantly disciplining himself, the yogī whose mind is controlled attains peace, the supreme nirvāṇa, which rests in me.
t.6.14: Serene in spirit and free from fear, steadfast in the vow of celibacy, having restrained the mind, with his thought fixed on me, he should sit disciplined, intent on me as the supreme goal.
t.6.16: Yoga is not for one who eats too much, nor for one who does not eat at all, O Arjuna; nor for one who is given to too much sleep, nor indeed for one who stays always awake.
t.6.17: For one who is moderate in food and recreation, moderate in his efforts in actions, and moderate in sleep and waking, yoga becomes the destroyer of sorrow.
t.6.18: When the well-restrained mind rests in the Self alone, free from longing for all desires, then one is said to be established in yoga.
t.6.19: As a lamp standing in a windless place does not flicker, such is the simile remembered for the yogin of controlled mind who practices the yoga of the self.
t.6.20: That state in which the mind, restrained by the practice of yoga, comes to rest, and in which, seeing the Self by the self, one is content in the Self alone.
t.6.21: When he knows that supreme bliss which is grasped by the intellect and lies beyond the senses, and, established therein, never moves away from the truth;
t.6.22: Having gained that, one thinks no other gain greater than it; established in that, one is not shaken even by heavy sorrow.
t.6.23: One should know that which is called yoga to be the disconnection from union with sorrow. This yoga should be practiced with determination, with a mind free from despondency.
t.6.24: Having completely abandoned all desires born of mental intention, and having restrained the whole host of the senses on every side by the mind alone,
t.6.25: Little by little one should come to rest, with the intellect held firm by steadfastness; having made the mind abide in the Self, one should think of nothing at all.
t.6.26: From whatever cause the restless and unsteady mind wanders away, from that very place he should restrain it and bring it under control in the Self alone.
t.6.27: Supreme happiness indeed comes to this yogin whose mind is perfectly tranquil, whose passion is stilled, who has become one with Brahman and is free from stain.
t.6.28: Thus constantly disciplining himself, the yogī, freed from impurity, easily attains the boundless happiness of contact with Brahman.
t.6.29: He whose self is joined in yoga, who sees the same everywhere, beholds the Self abiding in all beings and all beings in the Self.
t.6.30: One who sees me everywhere and sees everything in me, to him I am never lost, and he is never lost to me.
t.6.31: The yogī who, established in oneness, worships me as dwelling in all beings, abides in me, however he may live.
t.6.32: He who, by comparison with himself, sees equality everywhere, O Arjuna, whether in pleasure or in pain, that yogī is considered the highest.
t.6.33: Arjuna said: This yoga of evenness which you have taught, O Madhusūdana, I do not see its steady foundation, because of restlessness.
t.6.34: For the mind is restless, Kṛṣṇa, turbulent, and exceedingly strong; I consider restraining it to be as very difficult as restraining the wind.
t.6.35: The Blessed Lord said: Without doubt, O mighty-armed one, the mind is restless and hard to restrain; but by practice, O son of Kuntī, and by dispassion, it is held in check.
t.6.36: Yoga is hard to attain for one whose self is unrestrained; this is my view. But by one whose self is under control and who strives, it can be attained through the proper means.
t.6.37: Arjuna said: One who is endowed with faith but lacks self-control, whose mind has strayed from yoga, and who has not attained perfection in yoga, what destination does he reach, O Kṛṣṇa?
t.6.38: O mighty-armed one, does he not, fallen from both, perish like a scattered cloud, without support and bewildered on the path of Brahman?
t.6.39: This doubt of mine, O Kṛṣṇa, you ought to cut away completely, for no one other than you can be found who could dispel this doubt.
t.6.40: The Blessed Lord said: O Pārtha, neither here nor in the world beyond is there destruction for him; for no one who does good, my dear friend, ever goes to an evil end.
t.6.41: Having attained the worlds of those who have done good deeds and having dwelt there for countless years, the one who has fallen from yoga is born in the house of the pure and the prosperous.
t.6.42: Or else he is born into a family of wise yogins; for a birth such as this is very hard to obtain in this world.
t.6.43: There he regains that union with the understanding he had in his former body, and from that point he strives once more toward perfection, O joy of the Kurus.
t.6.44: By that very former practice he is carried onward, even without his will. Even one who merely seeks to know yoga goes beyond the Veda, the Brahman of sound.
t.6.45: But the yogī who strives with diligent effort, cleansed of all sin and perfected through many births, then attains the supreme goal.
t.6.46: The yogī is superior to the ascetics, and he is considered superior even to the men of knowledge; the yogī is also superior to the men of ritual action. Therefore, Arjuna, be a yogī.
t.6.47: And of all yogins, the one who, full of faith, worships me with his inner self gone to me, he is considered by me to be the most devoted in yoga.
